scams.name: SJO Airport Pirate-Taxi Cartel — $40 for a 4-Minute Ride & Worse
scams.description:
Cars are ORANGE (not the city's red), plates start with 'T' (TA, TSJ, TH, TP, TG), and the fare is fixed at a KIOSK INSIDE the terminal before you walk to the cab. Anyone outside the terminal quoting $20–$150 in a non-orange car is a pirata. They offer cheap fares, then meet accomplices along the route, assault passengers, steal everything, and dump them on the street.' One traveler: '$40 in a taxi to get 5 minutes from the airport. Driver gave us an insane price and when I called him out on it, he basically acknowledged it and said there's nothing I could do but pay.'; 20 minutes later they realized they were on the highway going the wrong way toward 'meeting people who were going to rob us.' (native Tico): 'Official taxis always start with T — TSJ, TA, TH, TP, TG + numbers. Regular private plates are six numbers or XXX 999.' The Uber variant: the traveler's driver dropped them at SJO, sped off WITHOUT ending the fare, drove loops, ended at ₡20,000 instead of the ₡3,900 quoted — a 5x gouge.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) at arrivals Ignore every 'taxi taxi' shout and anyone reaching for your bag —: 'if somebody unexpectedly picks up your bags… most likely going to lead to a scam or possibly something worse'; (2) walk to the Taxi Aeropuerto orange-kiosk IN the terminal (not the curb) — fare is ~$28–$33 to central San José / Paseo Colón, ~$40 to Escazú, ~$12–$18 to Alajuela hotels — and walk to the numbered orange cab they assign; (3) photograph the plate (must start with 'T') + driver's ID card BEFORE loading luggage; (4) alternative: pre-booked Interbus/Gray Line shuttle ($15–$25 pp shared) or hotel car (Intercontinental, Marriott Hacienda Belén offer free/paid shuttles); (5) Uber is often cheaper BUT gray-legal at SJO — sit up front to avoid airport-police notice, VERIFY driver ENDS the trip before you exit; (6) screenshot Uber quoted fare + pickup time; dispute any >2x overage with credit-card chargeback; (7) Don't accept a 'shared' ride at an unofficial curb pickup — the highway-shakedown pattern; emergency 911, US Embassy 2519-2000, OIJ 800-8000-645.
scams.avoidance: Pay at the Taxi Aeropuerto orange kiosk INSIDE the SJO terminal (~$28–$40 fixed). Verify plate starts with 'T' + photograph driver's ID + plate before loading bags. If Uber: sit up front, confirm driver ENDS the trip in app before you exit the vehicle. Pre-book Interbus/Gray Line ($15–$25 pp) or hotel shuttle as safest 1 AM option. Never accept a stranger's grab for your luggage — force them to put it down.
scams.location: Juan Santamaría International Airport (SJO / Alajuela) arrivals curb — exit lanes 1–8 immediately outside baggage claim; the informal 'bus station' pickup zone where pirate taxis cluster; late-night exits where the official orange-taxi kiosk is less staffed

scams.name: Fake Uber at SJO + Driver-Doesn't-End-Trip Fare Gouge
scams.description: The ARESEP transport regulator still officially considers rideshare illegal, and airport-taxi concessionaires actively police it at SJO. This grey zone creates two scam surfaces. First, the 'fake Uber' — a pirate-taxi driver stands at arrivals with a sign showing the rider's name (pulled from a social-media leak), and peels the tourist off the real Uber. (Oct 2025) and 'Late night Uber/transportation?' (2026) both document the 'driver cancels, friend-cousin-with-a-van steps in' pattern. Second, the 'driver doesn't end the fare' gouge: — One traveler paid ₡3,900 quoted, driver dropped them at SJO, sped off WITHOUT ending the ride, drove loops, ended at ₡20,000 — a 5x gouge.: 'Threaten Uber with a chargeback. Your credit card company will easily refund that.' One traveler: Arenal surge version — quoted ₡2,300, ended ₡9,800. Liberia: '$9 ride → $30 charge, over 16 km beyond actual drop-off,' refunded only after credit-card dispute. Third, the 'express kidnapping' tail: — the driver exited at drop-off, physically restrained the traveler, went through their pockets, and took $130 cash. sums the Tico view: 'At the airport take the orange taxis and everywhere else, just use Uber.': 'A friend paid about $200 for a ride because of a fraudulent driver (Uber refunded it). For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) when booking Uber at SJO meet the driver on the UPPER/DEPARTURES level (one traveler tip: 'find stairs up to go to departures, and the Uber will pick you up there') — airport police enforce against Uber at arrivals but not departures; (2) VERIFY the in-app plate matches the physical plate exactly; (3) ask the driver 'cuál es mi nombre?' — if they can't name you, it's a fake Uber; (4) at drop-off Don't EXIT until the driver taps 'End trip' and the receipt email arrives — if they speed off, screenshot the open trip and call Uber support immediately; (5) screenshot the quoted fare before the ride starts — proof for Uber and credit-card chargeback (Capital One, Chase Sapphire, Amex Platinum handle this well); (6) prefer DiDi or InDrive as cheaper gray-legal alternatives; (7) late-night solo: most respondents recommend orange taxi or hotel shuttle over Uber at that hour.
scams.avoidance: Meet Uber on the SJO DEPARTURES level (upstairs) not arrivals — escapes airport-police ban. Verify in-app plate MATCHES physical plate + ask 'cuál es mi nombre?' before entering. Watch driver 'End Trip' in the app + receipt email arrive before exiting the vehicle. Screenshot quoted fare + route in app; dispute overages with Uber + credit-card chargeback. Prefer DiDi or InDrive at equivalent prices; late-night solo: orange taxi or hotel shuttle.
scams.location: SJO arrivals curb, the departures-level Uber pickup stairs (the workaround to the airport-police ban), the Selina/Adventure Hostel pickup zone along Avenida 7 in San José Centro, and stops near Parque Morazán where Uber drivers canceling is common

scams.name: Claro / Kolbi SIM-Card 'Activation Fee' Fraud at SJO Baggage Claim
scams.description:
These guys are a fraud. They only accept cash and do not give change. They cannot give a receipt. They offer Claro's MOST EXPENSIVE pre-paid card as the "cheapest" pre-paid plan they have. The simcard you receive works for a couple of hours after which it gets blocked.' Follow-up: 'When we went to a Claro shop in San Jose the next day they told us the sim cards were not activated and thus we paid for nothing… and we needed to pay again.' one traveler noted a legit counter-example; clarified: 'Presumably the Claro shop employees do really sell the genuine thing… but from time to time they freeload on ignorant tourists like myself and keep the money for themselves.' Mechanics: real Claro/Kolbi prepaid SIMs with 5GB run ~₡5,000–₡10,000 (~$10–$20) at any in-city Claro or Kolbi store; the airport kiosk charges $25–$45 CASH ONLY, no receipt, sells an 'activated' SIM that dies after 2 hours, pockets the difference. A parallel TripAdvisor thread 'Scammed in Tamarindo Purchasing a SIM card' documents the same vendor network at beach kiosks. Legitimate 2025/2026 alternatives: Airalo eSIM (bought before flight, activates on landing, $4.50–$17 for 1–10GB, runs on Liberty/Claro); Kolbi SIM at Multiplaza Escazú, Mall San Pedro, or a Walmart phone counter; Liberty SIM at Liberty stores ($10–$12, 4GB). One traveler: 'In front of the airport you can find a Walmart… you can buy a sim card for $1.' describes a genuine Claro activation at a legit reseller — multiple photos of passport + arrival stamp, slow but legit, ₡10,000 for 2 SIMs.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) BEFORE your flight install Airalo ($4.50–$9 for 1–3GB/week or $17 for 10GB/30 days at airalo.com) — activates instantly on landing, eliminates the airport-kiosk trap; (2) alternatives: Holafly, Nomad, Maya Mobile — all eSIMs work on Liberty/Claro/Kolbi networks; (3) if your phone isn't eSIM-capable, SKIP the SJO Claro kiosk — the real Kolbi store at Multiplaza Escazú (15-min Uber) or any in-city Walmart's in-store phone counter sells a legit ₡5,000–₡10,000 SIM with proper registration; (4) if you must use the airport kiosk: INSIST on a printed receipt (required under Costa Rica Ley 7472); PAY BY CARD (Claro officially accepts Visa/Mastercard; cash-only is the scam signal); test the SIM with a WhatsApp message before leaving; (5) if scammed: screenshot the transaction; file at consumidor.go.cr (Ley 7472 violation) + SUTEL telecom regulator + credit-card chargeback; (6) SJO offers free Wi-Fi ('Free-Wifi-AeropuertoSJO') — you can coordinate your Uber/shuttle without buying a SIM at all.
scams.avoidance: Pre-install Airalo eSIM ($4.50–$17) BEFORE flight — skips the airport kiosk entirely. If SIM is required: wait and buy at Multiplaza Escazú Kolbi store or Walmart phone counter. At airport kiosk: demand printed receipt + pay only by Visa/Mastercard. Test SIM with WhatsApp message before leaving the kiosk — catches dead SIMs immediately. If scammed: file at consumidor.go.cr + SUTEL + credit-card chargeback (Ley 7472).
scams.location: Kiosk at SJO baggage-claim hall 1 (between the two carousels), the arrivals-area Claro counter opposite the currency-exchange booth, and the secondary Kolbi kiosk at departures pre-security

scams.name: SJO Rental-Car Counter 'Mandatory Insurance' $2,000 Ambush — Expedia / Hertz / Fox Trap
scams.description:
: One traveler bought 'FULL coverage insurance from Expedia' and paid ~$1,000 for 3 weeks; on arrival at the offsite lot was told either accept a $2,032 mandatory local insurance OR pay a $32,000 USD deposit with 20% deducted for any damage; when the traveler refused they were 'left on the side of the road with 5 suitcases.' Top reply: 'Adobe and Vamos come out on top every time, and warnings about not booking through third party sites like Expedia.': 'Even had this happen with Hertz.' One traveler: 'Same situation with me and Expedia and Fox Rental. Would not accept the Expedia insurance.' surfaces the legal reality, confirmed: 'The law says the only required insurance is third-party liability (SLI/TPL)… NOT REQUIRED is any collision damage coverage.' TPL in 2025/2026 runs ~$13–$20/day — anything above is optional. The scam runs two ways: (1) Expedia/Priceline/Kayak's advertised $19/day balloons at the counter with $25–$40/day mandatory insurance + $2,000 deposit hold — third-party CDWs routinely rejected; (2) Hertz/Fox/Budget/National SJO counters stack 'Super CDW' to push $29/day to $90/day.: 'If you decline CDW, you're required to bring proof of insurance from your credit card… don't forget the deposit — $2,000 for most rental companies.': 'Vamos and Adobe seem to be much more straightforward about using rental insurance from a credit card.' One traveler: '$700 for 10 day rental with Adobe including all insurance — they were amazing.'

For travelers 2025/2026: (1) Don't BOOK via Expedia, Priceline, Kayak, Hotwire, Travelocity — book DIRECT with Adobe (adobecar.com), Vamos (vamosrentacar.com), or Wildrider; online quotes include TPL and are transparent; (2) if using Hertz/Budget/National, email the CR counter for an all-in written quote before landing, and bring your credit-card's rental-coverage letter (Amex Premium, Chase Sapphire Reserve Primary, Capital One Venture X Primary) on bank letterhead — required to decline CDW legally; (3) CR requires TPL (~$13–$20/day) — accept it; above is optional unless your card doesn't cover CR (most do); (4) expect $1,500–$3,000 deposit hold clearing 7–14 days post-return; (5) PHOTOGRAPH every panel on pickup + return (video walk-around) — 'pre-existing damage' counter-scam runs often; (6) Adobe, Vamos, Alamo have ZERO counter-shakedowns reported 2024–2026; Hertz/Fox/Budget/Expedia have the worst profile; (7) file disputes at consumidor.go.cr + Amex/Visa chargeback.
scams.avoidance: Book DIRECT with Adobe, Vamos, or Wildrider — published all-in pricing, honored at counter. If using Hertz/Budget/National: email counter for written quote including TPL before landing. Bring printed credit-card CDW coverage letter (Amex Premium, Chase Sapphire Reserve Primary). Accept mandatory TPL only (~$13–$20/day) — decline CDW/Super CDW with written proof. Video walk-around on pickup + return; dispute via consumidor.go.cr + chargeback if ambushed.
scams.location: SJO airport rental-car shuttle zone (arrivals → van shuttle to off-airport lots); Adobe, Vamos, Economy, Alamo, Hertz, Fox, Budget, Enterprise, National, Sixt counters clustered on the service road along Route 1 just west of the terminal

scams.name: San José Airbnb / Rental Home-Invasion — The Calendar-Leak Pattern
scams.description:
OIJ data in NY Post (Dec 2, 2025) and Tico Times (Nov 26, 2025) shows over 6,300 crimes reported against tourists in 2024 alone. is the top anchor — the traveler's family held at gunpoint for 30 minutes at a Guanacaste Airbnb, 911 called, police arrived, gunfight erupted, one robber killed on the porch, two escaped. The traveler later wrote: 'They kept asking for the cocaine which was weird because we didn't have any. They had scoped out the house prior for sure.' Confirmed with a Teletica news link.: 'There's been a spree of robberies at Airbnb's over the past year or two.': 'a gang of thugs who have been terrorizing the area for months.' confirms a December Uvita Airbnb hit. details a Guanacaste home invasion where a tied-up couple endured a sexual assault 'she wasn't right to this day.', Tamarindo 5-year expat: 'We were robbed by the staff at first place we stayed while we were sleeping.': Playa Negra VRBO, 5–6 flashlights, alarm tripped, pile-furniture-in-bathroom defense — Vrbo refused refund. anchors the host-inside-job variant. Mechanics: Airbnb/VRBO public calendars telegraph arrival dates; scouts match addresses via Google Street View; 4–6-man gangs with handguns hit 9 PM–2 AM; isolated or weakly-gated homes in Escazú, Barrio Escalante, Santa Ana are high-profile targets. The US Embassy tells travelers: 'stay only at properties with continuous 24-hour professional security.' Canadian tourism fell 14% in H2 2025 (ticotimes.net, Dec 2025).

For travelers in San José 2025/2026: (1) book ONLY hotels with 24-hour armed guards — Hotel Grano de Oro (Barrio Amón), Intercontinental Real Costa Rica (Escazú), Hyatt Place San José, Marriott Hacienda Belén (near SJO), Hampton Inn SJO — all have verified 24/7 staff + CCTV; (2) if Airbnb, book ONLY inside a guarded gated community — Escazú porter-desk condos (Avenida Escazú, Distrito 4), Santa Ana's Río Oro or Forum Tower residences; (3) verify pre-booking in writing: '24/7 armed guard? CCTV?' — 'yes to all four' is the minimum bar; (4) calendar-block ±2 days on the host's public calendar; (5) never geo-tag the property on social media; (6) program 911, OIJ 800-8000-645, US Embassy 2519-2000 into speed dial on landing; (7) if invaded: hide, call 911, comply — OIJ confirms resistance correlates with shooting; file at Fuerza Pública + OIJ within 24h.
scams.avoidance: Book 24/7-guarded hotels in Escazú/Santa Ana/Barrio Amón — Intercontinental, Hyatt, Marriott. If Airbnb: inside a guarded gated community ONLY (Avenida Escazú, Río Oro, Forum Tower). Verify 24/7 guard + CCTV + panic button + patrol logs IN WRITING before booking. Calendar-block ±2 days on public calendar; never geo-tag the property on social media. If invaded: hide, 911, comply; file Fuerza Pública + OIJ within 24h for refund claim.
scams.location: Airbnbs and VRBOs across Escazú, Santa Ana, Barrio Escalante, Sabana Oeste, San Pedro, Curridabat, and the Central Valley outskirts — any property where the booking calendar publicly shows arrival dates, and isolated homes outside guarded communities

scams.name: Coca-Cola Bus Terminal Pickpocket & Luggage-Theft at the Zona Roja Edge
scams.description:
Canada's travel advisory (travel.gc.ca, 2025): 'Specific trouble spots include downtown San José areas near the Coca-Cola bus terminal, central market, and public parks.' Australia's Smartraveller: 'petty crime is common near the central bus terminal in the Coca Cola… most likely on weekends.' The zone is dense, unlit, and the hub for nearly every long-distance bus (Tracopa SJO→Jacó/Quepos; Alfaro SJO→Montezuma; MEPE SJO→Puerto Viejo; Empresarios Unidos SJO→Puntarenas). Pickpocket and luggage-lift crews work in 2–4-person cells — classic pattern: one person collides at the bus doorway, another lifts your daypack from the overhead rack, a third melts into the crowd. The canonical Reddit Tracopa case: — thieves planted as passengers wait for a rest stop, strip the bus of laptops/phones/passports from overhead bins, and vanish into a waiting car; one female passenger lost her laptop. One traveler: 'anything and everything with you if you want it when you return.' collects the urban variants:: 'Watch out for motorcyclists who can drive by and snatch a phone from your hand, or a necklace from your neck.' s Nueva York' warns: 'Plaza de la Cultura is safe during DAYLIGHT — pickpockets work the crowd.' Adjacent 'helpful stranger' scams: 'bird poop' on your shirt (sprayed by accomplice) + tissue + wallet lift; 'money on the ground' + two strangers claim it + your wallet vanishes during mediation.

For travelers 2025/2026: (1) Avoid Coca-Cola if possible — use Interbus (interbusonline.com) or Gray Line private shuttles ($49–$65 pp door-to-door, no terminal); (2) if using Tracopa/Alfaro/MEPE, arrive 15 minutes max ahead, stay inside the ticket office with bags on your lap, never accept 'help' with luggage from anyone not in company uniform; (3) SKIP Mercado Central and zona roja blocks north of Hotel Del Rey after dark; (4) on long-distance buses, never leave valuables in the overhead rack at a rest stop — daypack WITH you every time; (5) money belt for passport + 80% cash; decoy wallet in front pocket with expired card + ₡5,000; (6) phone on wrist-strap or zipped crossbody (Pacsafe); motorcycle-grab-from-stoplight is documented; (7) report at the Tourist Police Operations Center (San José hub opened 2025, English line) or OIJ 800-8000-645 within 24h.
scams.avoidance: Skip Coca-Cola: book Interbus/Gray Line private shuttle ($49–$65 pp, door-to-door). Never leave valuables in overhead bin during bus rest stops — carry daypack every time. Money belt under clothing for passport + 80% cash; decoy wallet in front pocket. Avoid Mercado Central / zona roja after dark; daylight only, nothing valuable in pockets. Tourist Police 24/7 hub (2025) + OIJ 800-8000-645 within 24h for insurance claim.
scams.location: Terminal 7-10 (Coca-Cola) and adjacent bus bays along Calle 14 / Avenida 1–5 in San José Centro; the Mercado Central five blocks south; the 'zona roja' (red-light) blocks immediately north of the terminal near Hotel Del Rey; nearby Tracopa, Alfaro, and MEPE bus bays

scams.name: Parque Central / Avenida 2 Cambista Currency-Exchange & 'Counterfeit Bill' Swap
scams.description:
In Parque Central, Avenida 2 pedestrian strip, and around Plaza de la Cultura, informal cambistas (money-changers) approach tourists with whispered 'cambio, cambio?' and a fan of colones. Three scams run. First, the rate gouge — the quoted rate is 10–20% below market (₡450 per USD) and the cambista talks fast to close before the tourist pulls out xe.com. Second, the counterfeit-bill swap — the cambista takes your $100 USD, fans out ₡50,000 in real colones, palms one ₡20,000 out during the count and replaces it with a crisp counterfeit that feels plastic-smooth. Third, the snatch-and-run — the cambista 'counts,' feigns a mistake, asks for the dollars back, hands them to an accomplice instead of the tourist, and both vanish. Tico Times 'Costa Rica Expat Living: My Encounter with Money Changers' (June 2023).: 'pay in colones (and beware of the "this bill is counterfeit" scam)' — drivers claim the ₡20,000 you handed is fake, pocket yours, hand back a prepared counterfeit, demand replacement.: 'Biggest scam is exchanging your money at the airport. The conversion rate is terrible. Just go to a major bank.' BCCR ATMs and Banco Nacional / BAC / Scotiabank / BCR branches post rates within 1% of market.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) Don't change money on the street — every whispered 'cambio' approach is a scam; (2) change at a bank branch with your passport, or withdraw colones from an in-branch ATM at a 1% spread; (3) pay shops, restaurants, taxis in COLONES not USD — removes the 'rounding' gouge; (4) check every ₡20,000 note: Carlos Luis Fallas watermark, a color-shifting security thread that flips green/blue when tilted, raised-print feel — counterfeits are smooth, lack the thread, don't flip colors; (5) if a cambista or driver claims your ₡20,000 is 'fake,' refuse to take it back and demand YOUR ORIGINAL visible in their hand — photograph it and call 911; the swap IS the scam; (6) use a no-FTF credit card (Capital One Venture, Chase Sapphire, Amex Platinum) for hotel + restaurants; colones cash only for taxis, tips, vendors; (7) BCCR ATM foreign-card limit ₡400,000/day (~$770); keep 3+ days of cash; (8) report at the San José Tourist Police Operations Center (2025) or OIJ 800-8000-645.
scams.avoidance: Never change money on the street — only bank branches or in-branch ATMs. Check ₡20,000 for Carlos Luis Fallas watermark + color-shift security thread. Refuse 'your bill is counterfeit' swap — keep YOUR original note visible + photograph it. Pay shops/taxis in COLONES (not USD) — removes the rounding-up gouge. Credit card (no-FTF Capital One/Chase/Amex) for hotels/restaurants; report at OIJ 800-8000-645.
scams.location: Parque Central San José (Avenida 2, Calle Central), Plaza de la Cultura edges, Avenida Central pedestrian strip between Calle 2 and Calle 9, the Correos de Costa Rica building cluster on Calle 2, and the casa de cambio clusters near Hotel Del Rey
